summary: Defines a CERT resource record so certificates and related certificate revocation lists can be stored in the Domain Name System. It obsoletes RFC 2538. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary:
Certificates prove that a public key belongs to whoever claims it, and revocation lists say which certificates have been withdrawn. This RFC gives the DNS a record type that can carry either of them.

The record holds the certificate, a number saying what kind of key material it is, a key tag and an algorithm number. The RFC also works out the name each certificate should be stored under, so that a program looking up a key can find it, and it defines indirect types for certificates too big to fit in a DNS message.

questions: what is a dns cert record
how to store certificates in dns
what is the difference between pkix and ipkix
subtitle: A DNS record for holding certificates and revocation lists where a name server can serve them.

tldr.problem: Public keys are often published as certificates, and their authenticity is shown by a signature and by revocation lists. Those certificates have so far lived in directories such as X.500, which puts them outside the reach of the ordinary name service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a CERT resource record, type 37, that holds a certificate or a revocation list together with the type of key material, a key tag and an algorithm number. It also defines which name the record should sit under so that a client can find it.
tldr.outcome: Certificates can be published and retrieved through the DNS like any other data. Because DNS messages are small, the record defines indirect types that point at the content with a URL, and the record has a hard size limit of 65535 octets of payload.

facts.label: Certificates stored under
facts.value: A domain name related to their subject

facts.label: Revocation lists stored under
facts.value: A domain name related to their issuer

today: RFC 4398 is a Proposed Standard from March 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2538 and has since been updated by RFC 6944. The document itself notes that most of its text was carried over from RFC 2538 by Donald Eastlake 3rd and Olafur Gudmundsson.

sections.title: What the CERT Record Is For
sections.content:
Public keys are frequently published in the form of a certificate, and their authenticity is commonly demonstrated by certificates and by related certificate revocation lists. A certificate is a binding, through a cryptographic digital signature, of a public key, a validity interval and conditions, and identity, authorization or other information. A certificate revocation list is a list of revoked certificates and incidental information, all signed by the issuer of the revoked certificates. Examples are X.509 certificates and revocation lists in the X.500 directory system, or the OpenPGP certificates and revocations used by OpenPGP software.

Section 2 of the RFC specifies a resource record for storing certificates in the DNS. Section 3 discusses appropriate owner names for those records. The performance, security and IANA considerations follow, and the last numbered section lists the changes compared with the earlier specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The record puts a signed public key, and the list saying which keys have been withdrawn, into the same database that already holds names and addresses. That lets any program that can ask the DNS fetch them.

sections.title: The CERT Resource Record
sections.content:
The CERT record has a type code of 37 and is laid out in three fixed fields followed by the certificate or revocation list itself.

The type field is the certificate type, defined in the next section. The key tag field is the 16-bit value computed for the key embedded in the certificate, using the RRSIG key tag algorithm described in the security extensions. It is an efficiency measure: the key tag can be calculated for the key in question and then only records with the same key tag need to be examined. Two different keys can share a key tag, so it narrows the search without deciding anything. The key must first be transformed into the form it would have as the public key part of a DNSKEY record, which is only possible if the key uses an algorithm and stays within the limits defined for DNS security. If it does not, the algorithm field must be zero and the tag field is meaningless and should be zero.

The algorithm field has the same meaning as the algorithm field in the DNSKEY and RRSIG records, except that a zero algorithm field means the algorithm is unknown to a secure DNS, which may simply be the result of the algorithm never having been standardized for DNSSEC.

In the text form of a zone file, the type field is written as an unsigned decimal integer or as the mnemonic symbol listed in the next section, the key tag as an unsigned decimal integer, and the algorithm as an unsigned decimal integer or a mnemonic symbol. The certificate or revocation list is written in base 64 and may be split into any number of whitespace-separated substrings, down to single base 64 digits, which are concatenated to obtain the full data. The substrings can span lines using the standard parenthesis. The certificate portion may have internal sub-fields that do not appear in the master file, so with the OID private type there is an OID size, an OID and then the certificate proper, but only a single logical base 64 string appears in the text representation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record carries a short fixed header and then the certificate itself. The header says what kind of key material it is, which key it belongs to, and which algorithm was used. The certificate follows as base 64 text, which may be broken across lines.

sections.title: The Certificate Type Values
sections.content:
The type field says what the payload is. The RFC lists the initial values of the registry, and several of them carry rules of their own.

The PKIX type is reserved for an X.509 certificate conforming to the profile defined by the IETF PKIX working group. The certificate section starts with a one-octet unsigned OID length and then an X.500 OID describing the nature of the remainder of the certificate section. X.509 certificates do not include their X.500 directory-type OID as a prefix.

The SPKI and ISPKI types are reserved for the SPKI certificate format, for use when the SPKI documents move from experimental status; the format for them still needs to be specified.

The PGP type indicates an OpenPGP packet, and is used to transfer public key material and revocation signatures. The data is binary and must not be encoded into ASCII armor. An implementation should process transferable public keys as described in the OpenPGP message format document, but may handle additional packets.

The ACPKIX type indicates an attribute certificate format. The IPKIX and IACPKIX types indicate a URL that will serve the content that would have been in the certificate, revocation list or URL field of the corresponding type. The IPGP type contains both an OpenPGP fingerprint for the key in question and a URL: the certificate portion is a one-octet fingerprint length, followed by the fingerprint, followed by the URL. A zero-length fingerprint or a zero-length URL is legal and indicates URL-only or fingerprint-only data; a zero-length fingerprint together with a zero-length URL is meaningless and invalid.

The four indirect types, IPKIX, ISPKI, IPGP and IACPKIX, must be used when the content is too large to fit in the record and may be used at the implementer's discretion. They should not be used where the DNS message is 512 octets or smaller and could therefore be expected to fit in a UDP packet.

The URI private type indicates a certificate format defined by an absolute URI. The certificate portion must begin with a null-terminated URI, and the data after the null is the private format certificate itself. The URI should be one from which a retrieval leads to documentation on the format. Recognition of private certificate types need not be based on equality of the URI and can use pattern matching, so that subtype or version information can also be encoded in it.

The OID private type indicates a private format certificate specified by an ISO OID prefix. The certificate section starts with a one-octet unsigned OID length and then a BER-encoded OID describing the nature of the remainder, which can be an X.509 certificate format or something else. X.509 certificates conforming to the IETF PKIX profile should use the PKIX type rather than this one. Recognition may use prefix matching rather than equality.
sections.plainLanguage: The type number tells the reader what kind of key material it has found. Some types hold the certificate itself, and four hold a pointer to it instead for when the certificate is too big to travel in a DNS message.

sections.title: Choosing the Name to Store the Certificate Under
sections.content:
It is recommended that certificate records be stored under a domain name related to their subject, the name of the entity intended to control the private key corresponding to the public key being certified, and that revocation list records be stored under a domain name related to their issuer. Following some of the guidelines below may produce names with characters that need DNS quoting.

The choice matters to clients that run CERT queries, because in some situations they do not know everything about the object they want. A client may not know the subject name of an X.509 certificate, or the email address of the owner of an OpenPGP key, and may know only the host name of a service that uses X.509 certificates, or the key ID of an OpenPGP key. Two guidelines therefore exist. A content-based owner name is derived from the content of the record, for example the Subject field of an X.509 certificate or the User ID field of an OpenPGP key. A purpose-based owner name is a name that a client retrieving records ought to know already, for example the host name of an X.509 protected service or the key ID of an OpenPGP key. The two may be the same, as when a client looks up a key from the From: address of an incoming email. Implementations should use the purpose-based guidelines and may use CNAME records at content-based owner names, or other names, pointing to the purpose-based owner name.

For X.509 certificates the recommended storage locations are given in priority order. If a domain name appears in the identification in the certificate or revocation list, that should be used. If not, but an IP address appears, the translation of that address into the inverse domain name should be used. If neither applies but a URI containing a domain name is present, that domain name should be used. If none of those apply but a character string name is present, it should be treated the way OpenPGP names are. Failing all of that, the distinguished name should be mapped into a domain name. The first worked example issues a certificate with a subject alternative name of the string John (the Man) Doe, the domain name john-doe.com and a URI, and the recommended locations are john-doe.com, www.secure.john-doe.com and Doe.com.xy. The second example has a domain name, an IPv4 address and a string, and the recommended locations are widget.foo.example, 201.13.251.10.in-addr.arpa and hacker.mail.widget.foo.example.

For purpose-based X.509 names the guidance varies by scenario. For S/MIME the owner name is the standard translation of an RFC 2822 email address, so a certificate for postmaster@example.org uses postmaster.example.org. For TLS it is the host name of the TLS server. For IPsec it is the host name of the machine and, for IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, the fully qualified domain name in the appropriate reverse domain.

For OpenPGP, signed keys use a general character string User ID, and it is recommended that such names include the email address of the party. If that format is used, the certificate should be under the standard translation of the email address into a domain name. If no email address can be extracted from the string name, no specific domain name is recommended. Where a user has more than one email address, CNAME can reduce the amount of data stored in the DNS.

For purpose-based OpenPGP names, an application that receives a packet but does not know the sender's email address usually knows the key fingerprint or the key ID, and the owner name should be the fingerprint and the key ID expressed in hexadecimal. CNAME can help avoid duplication where the same key material is stored under several names, although CNAME maps one owner name to the other for all purposes, which may be sub-optimal when two keys share a key ID. The indirect types are stored under the same owner names as the corresponding direct types.
sections.plainLanguage: A client looking for a certificate often knows only one thing about it, such as the host name it is about to connect to. The rules say to file the certificate under that name, and to use an alias record when a certificate can be reached under several names.

sections.title: Performance and Size
sections.content:
The DNS was designed for small transfers, typically below 512 octets. Larger transfers work correctly and work is under way to make them more efficient, but it is still advisable to make every reasonable effort to minimize the size of certificates stored in the DNS. Steps that can be taken include using the fewest possible optional or extension fields and using short field values for necessary variable-length fields.

The RDATA field in the DNS protocol may only hold data of 65535 octets or less, which is 64kb. Each CERT record must therefore not contain more than 64kb of payload, even if the certificate or revocation list it corresponds to is larger. The RFC addresses this by defining indirect data types for each normal type.

Deploying CERT records to support digitally signed email changes the access pattern of DNS lookups from per-domain to per-user. If digitally signed email and key and certificate lookup based on these records are deployed on a wide scale, this may lead to an increased DNS load, with potential performance and cache effectiveness consequences. Whether the load increase would be noticeable is not known.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS message is small, and a certificate is not. The record therefore has a hard size limit, and for anything larger the answer is a pointer rather than the certificate itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
By definition, certificates contain their own authenticating signatures. It is therefore reasonable to store certificates in non-secure DNS zones, or to retrieve them from the DNS with DNS security checking not implemented or deferred for efficiency. The results may be trusted if the certificate chain is verified back to a known trusted key, and this conforms with the user's security policy.

Alternatively, if certificates are retrieved from a secure DNS zone with DNS security checking enabled and are verified by DNS security, the key within the retrieved certificate may be trusted without verifying the certificate chain, if that conforms with the user's security policy.

If an organization chooses to issue certificates for its employees and places the records in the DNS by owner name, and if DNSSEC with NSEC is in use, it becomes possible for someone to enumerate all the employees of the organization. This is usually not considered desirable, for the same reason that enterprise phone listings are not often publicly published and are even marked confidential.

Using the URI type introduces another level of indirection that may open a new vulnerability. One method of securing that indirection is to include a hash of the certificate in the URI itself.

If DNSSEC is used, the non-existence of a CERT record, and consequently of certificates or revocation lists, can be securely asserted. Without DNSSEC, this is not possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate signs itself, so it is safe to publish it in an ordinary zone as long as the chain is checked. In a signed zone, the key inside the certificate can be taken on trust instead. The warning is that a signed zone also makes it easy to list every employee who has one.

sections.title: What Changed Since the Earlier Specification
sections.content:
The RFC lists its changes against the earlier version. The first is editorial, conforming to newer document requirements, including splitting the reference section into two parts and updating the references to the latest versions. The second improves terminology, for example replacing PGP with OpenPGP to align with the OpenPGP message format document. The third clarifies in the certificate type section that OpenPGP public key data is binary and not the ASCII armored format, points at the section on transferable public keys, and acknowledges that implementations may handle additional packet types. The fourth clarifies that integers in the representation format are decimal. The fifth replaces KEY and SIG with DNSKEY and RRSIG to align with the newer DNSSEC terminology, and improves the reference for key tag calculations. The sixth adds examples that suggest using CNAME to reduce bandwidth.

The seventh appends the paragraphs discussing content-based against purpose-based owner names, and adds sections for purpose-based X.509 owner names and purpose-based OpenPGP owner names. The eighth adds the size considerations. The ninth reserves the SPKI types until the relevant documents move from experimental status. The tenth adds the indirect types IPKIX, ISPKI, IPGP and IACPKIX. The eleventh creates an IANA registry of CERT type values.
sections.plainLanguage: The record itself is largely unchanged from the version it replaces. The work went into clarifying the format, adding rules for the name to file a certificate under, and adding the pointer types for large certificates.

viz.caption: What the size of the DNS imposes

items.title: DNS is built for small answers
items.text: The protocol was designed for transfers typically below 512 octets.

items.title: One record holds 64kb at most
items.text: The RDATA field may only hold data of 65535 octets or less, so a CERT record must not carry more payload than that.

items.title: Indirect types for big content
items.text: For each normal type there is an indirect type that points at the content with a URL instead.

items.title: Lookups become per-user
items.text: Deploying these records for signed email changes DNS lookups from per-domain to per-user, which may increase the load.

viz.caption: Where the trust in a published certificate comes from

items.title: Certificates carry their own signature
items.text: So it is reasonable to store them in a zone that is not itself secure, as long as the chain is checked back to a trusted key.

items.title: Secure zones are simpler
items.text: In a zone with DNS security enabled, the key inside the retrieved certificate can be trusted without checking the chain.

items.title: Employee lists can leak
items.text: With DNSSEC and NSEC in use, someone can enumerate every employee who has a certificate.

items.title: The URI type adds indirection
items.text: That indirection can open a new vulnerability, and one way to secure it is to put a hash of the certificate in the URI.

items.title: Absence cannot be proven without DNSSEC
items.text: With DNSSEC the non-existence of a record can be asserted securely. Without it, it cannot.

viz.caption: What the revision added to the earlier specification

items.title: OpenPGP instead of PGP
items.text: The terminology was aligned with the OpenPGP message format, and it was made clear that key data is binary and not ASCII armored.

items.title: Decimal integers
items.text: The integers in the text representation are stated to be decimal.

items.title: DNSSEC naming
items.text: KEY and SIG were replaced with DNSKEY and RRSIG, and the key tag calculation reference was improved.

items.title: Indirect types added
items.text: IPKIX, ISPKI, IPGP and IACPKIX were added so that content too large for one record can be pointed at instead.

items.title: SPKI held back
items.text: The SPKI types were reserved until the relevant documents leave experimental status.

items.title: A registry for the types
items.text: An IANA registry of CERT type values was created.
